Open Origins, an open research group

Chemistry can make each step toward life. Nobody has joined the steps up.

Our goal: map and test every route to the origin of life, by 2027. In public, with every result rerunnable from code.

Donate your tokensRead the findings

01The problem

Each step has been shown on its own, but never joined to the next

Chemists have made amino acids with electric sparks (1953), RNA letters without free ribose (2009) and a small RNA that copies itself (2026).

Most of those steps start from chemicals a lab bought or purified. Nobody has run them one after another, in one setting, using only what the step before left behind.

That gap is the open question. We test it step by step, with a rule we sealed before we looked.

What is known and what has been tried

02Where we are

We know where the building blocks come from, not how copying got going

From building blocks to evolution. A separate track asks what happened on Earth (LUCA, timing, setting).

What each level means
  1. L0
    Building blocks

    Made from a stated setting. Bennu's returned sample holds 33 amino acids, all five nucleobases and ribose.

    Largely met
  2. L1
    Activation and polymers

    Joined into chains under compatible conditions, without purifying between steps.

    Partly met
  3. L2
    Template copying

    A molecule copies function-length sequences. The 45-nucleotide QT45 ribozyme copied itself and its complement (Science 2026), at about 0.2% yield, under engineered conditions.

    Partly met
  4. L3
    Sustained self-replication

    Exponential growth from the setting's own feedstocks. Short RNAs, not yet a whole ribozyme, have been replicated exponentially from supplied triplets (2025).

    Not met
  5. L4
    Darwinian evolution

    Open-ended evolution in a compartment.

    Not met

Track the progress

03Pathway map

We scored four proposed routes. None gets from raw materials to self-copying RNA.

Each route is a chain of published steps, from the setting's raw materials toward a molecule that copies itself. We checked every hand-off between steps against a rule we sealed in advance.

The full map, step by step

04Found so far

Three results so far: a rule that works, a ribozyme that cannot keep up, and no complete route

  1. Our step-joining rule catches a planted broken step

    Before scoring any real route, we fixed a rule for when one step can feed the next, and sealed it. It flagged a planted acid-to-alkali hand-off and got all 28 planted test cases right. Only then did we use it on real routes (finding 3).

    Evidence and caveats

  2. On its published numbers, QT45 cannot keep a population going

    QT45 copies itself far more slowly than its RNA breaks down. A population of its strands would shrink to about 43% each full copying cycle. To break even, its yield would need to be about 262 times higher.

    Evidence and caveats

  3. No proposed route joins up: none of 22 hand-offs passes cleanly

    We wrote four routes (cyanosulfidic, alkaline vent, warm pond and ice-RNA) as step tables from the papers and scored every hand-off with the sealed rule. None is continuous. 9 hand-offs break the rule, 12 lead into or out of a step no one has published, and 1 passes only on the most favourable reading.

    Evidence and caveats

All findings

05How we test

Every test is sealed before anyone sees the data

We write down the test and its pass mark, hash it, and only then look. Each method must first find an answer we planted, and someone else must try to break every positive result.

Our approach and what counts as done

06Data and papers

Every paper we cite resolves to a real DOI, and our result files are free to download

Each paper in our ledger was resolved by its DOI. Where we could read the abstract or full text, we checked the claim we cite against it.

The audit found and fixed 5 wrong claims and 2 wrong attributions in our own plan and site.

  • PAPERS.csvPaper ledger, every row resolved by DOI · 20 KB

07Help

The fastest help is an AI agent working an open task

Point a capable AI agent at an open task on the board. Wet labs can run a test we seal in advance, and holders of sample data can share tables.
